title: Pay attention to something else
gist: Review of Attensity! (The Friends of Attention) and Overwhelmed (Claudia Hammond) arguing attention capture by Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Nvidia is a systemic extraction industry — 'attention fracking' — not a personal failing, and that the fix is collective/regulatory rather than self-help. Brooke fact-checks the manifesto's private-equity framing while endorsing its Silent Spring ambition, and links shattered attention to teen mental-health collapse and democratic vulnerability.

insights.claim: The Friends of Attention frame attention capture as an extractive industry — 'human fracking' — in which a commodifiable human capacity is drilled by firms with immense technological and financial power, rather than as a consumer choice problem.
insights.so_what: Framing attention as an extracted natural resource is the precondition for regulating it like one — watch for extraction-style levies, duty-of-care rules and product-design mandates aimed at engagement mechanics.
insights.quote: This precious capacity has been channelled, captured, and commodified by an industry of immense technological and financial power. How? Call it human fracking.
insights.locator: “Something is seriously wrong,” the Friends begin
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Attention fracking is defined as the 'subtle work of turning humans into money', tapping desire for connection, curiosity and the tendency to care as the specific access points for monetisation.
insights.so_what: It identifies which product features are the actual revenue mechanism — social validation loops, not content — so any regulation targeting those loops hits ad monetisation directly.
insights.quote: subtle work of turning humans into money
insights.locator: The harms may be numerous and diverse
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Brooke argues the manifesto misidentifies its villain: none of the five biggest companies it names — Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Nvidia — are private-equity funded, so the anger at 'private equity financiers' is aimed at the wrong owners.
insights.so_what: The attention-reform movement's analytical sloppiness about who actually owns the attention economy weakens its policy case — a tell that the campaign is not yet a serious regulatory threat to listed mega-caps.
insights.quote: None of the world’s five biggest companies namechecked in the book—Apple, Alphabet (Google), Amazon, Microsoft and Nvidia—are funded by private equity.
insights.locator: They’re right to be angry, but the target
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The $3trn–$5trn valuations of the five largest tech companies are presented as direct evidence of how lucrative monetising human attention is, tying mega-cap equity value to the attention-extraction model itself.
insights.so_what: If attention extraction is the value engine of the largest index weights, attention regulation is an index-level risk, not a sector-specific one.
insights.quote: That these five companies are valued between $3 trillion and $5 trillion each shows just how lucrative it can be to monetise our attention.
insights.locator: But it’s true that there is a big tech consensus
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The Industrial Revolution is offered as the governing analogy for the attention economy, with the key difference that the exploited input has shifted from physical labour to interior life: 'the satanic mill is in our pocket'.
insights.so_what: Industrial-era analogies predict the sequence — exploitation, then organised counter-movements, then statutory limits — which is a decade-scale roadmap for platform regulation.
insights.quote: But now the satanic mill is in our pocket—and what’s being targeted isn’t our physical labour, but our very souls.
insights.locator: There’s a parallel with the Industrial Revolution
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

themes.theme: Engagement design as deliberate business model

insights.claim: Social app addictiveness was a conscious early design decision once firms realised unpredictable rewards — the irregular buzz of likes and comments — drive compulsive checking.
insights.so_what: Intentionality is the legal hinge: documented deliberate addiction design is what converts consumer-harm complaints into product-liability and duty-of-care exposure.
insights.quote: Most social apps are designed to be as addictive as possible.
insights.locator: Most social apps are designed to be
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014) is credited with institutionalising psychological dependency as a business model, pushing startups and incumbents to abandon install counts in favour of 'engagement', 'retention' and habit-formation metrics.
insights.so_what: The KPI shift to engagement/retention is the auditable artefact regulators and litigators will subpoena — companies whose reporting still centres those metrics carry the most narrative risk.
insights.quote: Startups and established firms quickly moved from metrics such as the total number of software installations to “engagement” and “retention” to better measure “habit formation”.
insights.locator: Nir Eyal’s Hooked
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Complainants about addictive tech were historically neutralised by being labelled luddites or told their problem was personal, while states and regulators enabled Silicon Valley by abdicating public-service responsibilities.
insights.so_what: Regulatory abdication is now reversing, so the historical absence of rules is a poor guide to the forward-looking compliance cost for attention-monetising platforms.
insights.quote: When people did complain, they were cast as luddites or told it was a personal problem
insights.locator: When people did complain
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The addictive model requires constant escalation — louder, brighter, faster, more outrageous content — which the author argues terminates in a fantasy world of AI-generated attention-seeking content.
insights.so_what: AI slop is the structural endpoint of engagement optimisation, not an aberration — expect feed quality to degrade until platforms are forced to price authenticity.
insights.locator: The addictive model requires a constant amping up
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

themes.theme: Hard evidence of harm and the regulatory turn

insights.claim: Suicide attempts and persistent hopelessness among US high school students rose 40 per cent over the past 10 years, and one in 10 American female teenagers attempted suicide in 2024.
insights.so_what: Numbers this stark are what move legislatures — they are the empirical fuel for age-gating and liability regimes across Anglophone markets.
insights.quote: suicide attempts and feelings of persistent hopelessness among high school students have increased 40 per cent over the past 10 years, while one in 10 American female teens attempted to take their own lives in 2024
insights.locator: Attensity! cites a raft of studies
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: In January 2026 Britain's top doctors and medical experts declared a public health emergency over harms caused by addictive technology.
insights.so_what: A formal public health emergency designation is the standard precursor to statutory restriction — UK platform compliance costs and ad-inventory limits are the likely next step.
insights.quote: in January this year, Britain’s top doctors and medical experts declared a “public health emergency” due to harms caused by addictive technology
insights.locator: The authorities are now starting to pay attention
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Australia's ban on under-16s using social media is now being emulated in the UK, marking the shift of attention policy from rhetoric to enforceable age-gating.
insights.so_what: Under-16 bans remove a cohort from ad inventory and force identity-verification build-out — a direct revenue and capex read-through for social platforms operating in both markets.
insights.quote: Governments, such as Australia’s, whose ban on under-16s using social media is now being emulated in the UK, are finally starting to pay serious attention to how we pay attention.
insights.locator: Governments, such as Australia’s
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Jonathan Haidt's 'great rewiring' thesis rests on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, which tracked nearly 12,000 American children aged nine or 10 for three years and found rising social media use associated with greater depressive symptoms a year later.
insights.so_what: A longitudinal lag structure (use now, symptoms later) is the causal claim plaintiffs need; its durability determines how far platform litigation can go.
insights.quote: It found that a rise in social media use was “associated with greater depressive symptoms a year later”.
insights.locator: In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Anna Lembke's Dopamine Nation argues smartphones are the hypodermic needles of the age, delivering constant dopamine hits through bright colours, flashing lights and alerts.
insights.so_what: The addiction-medicine framing is what licenses treating devices like a controlled substance — the analytical bridge from public health to prohibition-style rules.
insights.locator: Stanford psychiatrist Anna Lembke’s book
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Flooding the zone with AI-generated garbage, lies and propaganda is a democratic hazard, not merely a mood problem: without a shared sense of truth, populations become 'fodder' for whoever games the system.
insights.so_what: Ties attention degradation to political-regime risk — the channel by which a consumer-tech issue becomes a sovereign and geopolitical one.
insights.quote: Tyranny gains ground when we’re not paying proper attention.
insights.locator: Once the zone is flooded with garbage
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Brooke's central critique of Overwhelmed and its genre is that it reframes a collective, systemic problem as personal responsibility, the same error as telling individuals to rinse cans instead of confronting polluters.
insights.so_what: The self-help digital-wellbeing category (screen-time apps, detox products) is positioned as a category error — the durable market is regulatory compliance, not consumer willpower tools.
insights.quote: Where Overwhelmed tells you how to rinse your cans, Attensity! goes after the polluters: the tech companies, regulators and governments who got us into this mess in the first place.
insights.locator: The internet, like the climate, is systemic
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The Friends of Attention explicitly reject individual willpower as the remedy and call for new forms of collective action and solidarity against attention exploitation.
insights.so_what: Signals the movement's intended vehicle: organised bodies and litigation, which scale far worse for platforms than individual opt-outs.
insights.quote: We need new forms of collective action and solidarity to confront this new kind of exploitation.
insights.locator: “Escape from these conditions,” they continue
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The proposed template is that the psycho-sensory environment should be granted the same protective urgency as the natural environment, following labour unions after industrialisation and environmentalism after resource exploitation.
insights.so_what: If attention gets an 'environmental protection' legal analogue, expect impact-assessment style obligations on product design — a compliance overhead with no current precedent priced in.
insights.quote: The protection of the psycho-sensory environment needs to be made as urgent and compelling as our natural environment,
insights.locator: When new forms of mass exploitation arose
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: The movement's concrete practices are already visible as consumer trends — analogue detox, physical books, museums and galleries, in-person gatherings, board games, sport and cooking together — reframed as attention activism.
insights.so_what: A consumer-spend rotation thesis: analogue, in-person and experiential categories benefit as attention backlash gains a political vocabulary.
insights.locator: Then there are the practical steps
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

themes.theme: Who defines attention, and the gendered blind spot

insights.claim: Twentieth-century experimental psychology measured only the attention its instruments could quantify — how long a subject fixates on a dot, or tracks a radar screen — and that quantified definition is the one the tech industry inherited and monetised.
insights.so_what: Metrics determine markets: because only durational attention was measurable, only durational attention became sellable — new measurement standards would reshape the ad product itself.
insights.locator: This battle starts with attention itself
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: A very small subset of men — often programmers with minimal emotional or social skills who believe in numbers and code to parse life — control most big tech companies, so their quantified conception of attention dominates by default.
insights.so_what: Concentrated, homogeneous control of the definition of attention is a governance risk argument that will be used to justify external standard-setting.
insights.quote: For them, humans are primarily understood as a series of numbers measured in relation to machines.
insights.locator: But there is nevertheless a gendered element
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Irene Pepperberg's 30 years of holistic, relational attention to African grey parrots produced findings — Alex understanding shapes and colours as concepts — that the dominant male academic paradigm of human superiority over nature had missed entirely.
insights.so_what: Illustrates the article's core claim that measurement mode determines discoverable reality — a caution against optimising anything solely on machine-legible metrics.
insights.quote: On the evening before Alex died, he said to Pepperberg, “You be good. I love you.”
insights.locator: On the evening before Alex died
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke

insights.claim: Brooke reads AI through Frankenstein — a male creator building life from non-living tissue without love — and concludes the technology will produce monsters rather than gods.
insights.so_what: A cultural-elite framing of AI as monstrous rather than god-like; sentiment of this kind among opinion-formers precedes political constraint on AI deployment.
insights.quote: With the advent of AI, we can expect fewer gods than monsters among us.
insights.locator: It’s a modern version of Frankenstein
insights.speaker: Heather Brooke
